mkt-geo-1:x:1.prompt: What does GEO (Generative Engine Optimization) refer to?
choices: Optimizing content to get cited in the answers of generative AIs
Optimizing a site for location-based searches on Google Maps
Automatically generating optimized pages with a generative AI
A new HTML markup standard for AI-generated content
mkt-geo-1:x:1.explain: GEO aims to get cited in generated answers, whereas SEO aims to rank in a list of links. The two overlap, but GEO mainly rewards the clarity, authority and "citability" of a passage.

mkt-geo-1:x:2.prompt: What is the main difference between SEO and GEO?
choices: SEO aims for a rank among links; GEO, for a citation in an answer
GEO only covers AI-powered image and video search results
SEO is paid per click, while GEO remains entirely free
None: GEO is just the new marketing name for SEO
mkt-geo-1:x:2.explain: In a generated answer there are no ten positions: there are a few cited sources. Being "well ranked" is no longer enough, you have to be the source the model chooses to pick up.

mkt-geo-1:x:3.prompt: Which of these signals helps a passage most to get cited by an AI?
choices: A direct answer in 2 or 3 sentences, under an explicit heading
A long introductory paragraph before getting to the point
The main keyword repeated in every sentence of the passage
A very long passage that covers every aspect of the topic
mkt-geo-1:x:3.explain: Generative engines extract passages. A short block that answers the question asked by the heading on its own can be cited without rewriting, which is exactly what the model is looking for.

mkt-geo-1:x:4.prompt: What does "Information Gain" mean for a piece of content?
choices: It brings information that other sources don't have
It is longer and more complete than competing pages
It contains more outbound links to reliable sources
It was published or updated more recently than the rest
mkt-geo-1:x:4.explain: Content that repeats what ten others already say has no reason to be chosen. A new data point, a real test, an original figure give the model a reason to cite you.

choices: AI-generated answers at the top of the results, with their sources
A paid Google tool for analyzing a website's audience
A new video ad format shown at the top of the results
The name of the bot that crawls and indexes pages for Google
mkt-geo-1:x:5.explain: AI Overviews (formerly SGE) synthesize an answer above the classic links. Being cited there captures a share of the traffic that organic results lose (zero-click).

mkt-geo-1:x:6.prompt: Why do brand mentions (even without a link) matter in GEO?
choices: AIs associate brand and topic from the whole web, links or not
Google automatically counts them as dofollow backlinks
They pass on PageRank, just like a regular followed link
They don't count: only links have any influence on AI models
mkt-geo-1:x:6.explain: An LLM doesn't need a link to connect your brand to a topic: it only needs the association to appear often in its data. Textual brand awareness becomes a lever in its own right.

mkt-geo-1:x:7.prompt: An llms.txt file at the root of the site guarantees being cited by AIs.
choices: True
False
mkt-geo-1:x:7.explain: llms.txt is a proposal to guide models toward your important content. Useful and cheap, but no engine guarantees reading it, let alone citing you.

mkt-geo-1:x:8.prompt: Structured data (schema.org) helps generative engines understand a page.
choices: True
False
mkt-geo-1:x:8.explain: Markup makes the content type explicit (FAQ, product, author, review). The search pipelines of generative engines rely heavily on the classic index, where this markup matters.

mkt-geo-1:x:9.prompt: Put the steps to optimize a page for GEO in order
steps: Identify the questions people ask AIs about the topic
Write a direct, self-contained answer under each question, used as a heading
Add a piece of new information (data, example, first-hand experience)
Mark up the page (author, FAQ, dates) and make it easy to crawl
Check in ChatGPT / Perplexity whether the page is cited, and adjust
mkt-geo-1:x:9.explain: You start from real demand, structure for extraction, make yourself unique, make yourself readable, then measure. Without the final measurement, you never know whether it works.

mkt-case-1:x:1.title: Traffic collapses
mkt-case-1:x:1.scenario: You manage the blog of a small business. For 3 weeks, organic traffic has dropped by 40%. Search Console shows no manual penalty. Rankings have fallen on almost every query, not just a few.

steps.prompt: What is the first thing to check?
choices: A Google algorithm update on the same dates
Buying backlinks to make up for the lost rankings
Rewriting every blog page with an AI
Raising the Google Ads budget to fill the traffic gap
steps.feedback: A broad, simultaneous drop with no manual penalty almost always points to a core update. You date the drop and compare it with the update calendar.

steps.prompt: The drop coincides with a core update. You notice your articles mostly repeat what competitors say. What do you do?
choices: Enrich the key pages with original data and case studies
Publish more short articles on the same topics to cover the ground
Delete all the articles and start again from a blank blog
Wait for the next update without changing anything
steps.feedback: Core updates reward helpful, original content (E-E-A-T, information gain). Volume doesn't help; added value does.

steps.prompt: When should you measure the effect of your changes?
choices: At the next core update, in a few weeks or months
The next day, as soon as Google has recrawled the pages
Never: the effect of content can't be measured
After migrating the site to a new CMS
steps.feedback: The effects of a core update are mostly re-evaluated at the next one. You keep improving, track rankings, and judge over several weeks.

mkt-case-1:x:1.explain: Diagnosis (date it, cross-check with updates), treatment (quality and originality), measurement (patience and tracking). The "buy links" reflex almost always makes things worse.

mkt-case-1:x:2.title: The Ads budget is burning
mkt-case-1:x:2.scenario: A Google Ads Search campaign spends €2,000 / month. The CTR is fine (5%), but the conversion rate is 0.3% and the CPA is exploding. The landing page is the site's homepage.

steps.prompt: Where is the most likely problem?
choices: After the click: the homepage doesn't keep the ad's promise
Before the click: the ads don't attract enough clicks
The keywords aren't generating enough impressions
The budget is too small for the algorithm to learn
steps.feedback: A good CTR with poor conversion points to the landing page. A generic homepage doesn't convert a specific intent.

steps.prompt: What do you set up first?
choices: A dedicated landing page per ad group, with a single CTA
A newsletter sign-up pop-up on the current homepage
Switching to broad match keywords to reach more people
A company presentation video at the top of the homepage
steps.feedback: Ad → page consistency, a single message, a single call to action: that's the foundation of CRO for paid.

steps.prompt: How do you check that the new page performs better?
choices: An A/B test with enough traffic to be significant
Comparing conversions by gut feeling after two days
Asking the team which version they prefer
Looking only at how the ads' CTR changes
steps.feedback: You test, wait for statistical significance, and decide on the conversion rate, not on impressions.

mkt-case-1:x:2.explain: Good CTR + poor conversion = page problem, not ad problem. Dedicated landing page, one CTA, A/B test.

mkt-case-1:x:3.title: Choosing your keywords
mkt-case-1:x:3.scenario: You're launching the blog of an AI consulting firm for small businesses. You have two candidates: "artificial intelligence" (110,000 searches / month, huge competition) and "integrate chatgpt in a small business" (400 searches / month, little competition).

steps.prompt: Which keyword should you start with?
choices: The long tail: "integrate chatgpt in a small business"
"artificial intelligence", for its huge search volume
Both at the same time on the same page
Neither: SEO doesn't work anymore
steps.feedback: A new site won't rank on a generic query against Wikipedia and major media. The long tail has less volume, but a precise intent and a real chance of ranking.

steps.prompt: How do you structure the content around this keyword?
choices: A pillar page plus satellite articles linked to each other
Ten near-identical articles, each on a variation of the keyword
A single short 200-word page focused on the keyword
One page per synonym, with no links at all between them
steps.feedback: The topic cluster shows Google expertise on the whole subject, and internal linking channels authority toward the pillar page.

steps.prompt: Three months later, the pillar page is in position 4. Which lever gets it into the top 3?
choices: Earning a few relevant backlinks and adding a client case study
Repeating the keyword 30 more times on the page
Buying 500 links on directories to speed things up
Changing the domain name so it contains the keyword
steps.feedback: Authority (quality links) + added value (information gain). Keyword stuffing and link farms are penalized.

mkt-case-1:x:3.explain: Long tail first, topic cluster next, authority and originality to finish.

mkt-case-1:x:4.prompt: Your email open rate drops from 35% to 12% in one week, with no change in subject lines or frequency. Most likely cause?
choices: Deliverability: sender reputation or SPF / DKIM / DMARC
All subscribers lost interest in the brand in the same week
The main CTA is badly placed in the body of the email
The logo changed in the email header
mkt-case-1:x:4.explain: A sudden, across-the-board drop in open rate almost always means you're landing in spam. Check authentication, domain reputation and blacklists before touching the content.

mkt-case-1:x:5.prompt: Your product page has an 85% bounce rate from a Meta Ads campaign. What do you look at first?
choices: Whether the first screen keeps the ad's promise
The total number of indexed pages on the site
The color and size of the buy button
The number of followers of the brand's Meta page
mkt-case-1:x:5.explain: A massive bounce from a single traffic source points to an ad → page mismatch (or a page that's too slow on mobile). Start with message consistency and load time.

mkt-case-2:x:1.title: Getting cited by ChatGPT
mkt-case-2:x:1.scenario: You're a GEO consultant for an accounting firm. The client wants ChatGPT and Perplexity to cite them for the question "which accountant for a start-up in Lyon?". Their site: 40 service pages, never any original content, no mentions anywhere else on the web.

steps.prompt: Which project should you start with?
choices: Creating content that answers the questions people ask AIs
Buying 200 backlinks to gain authority quickly
Adding an llms.txt file at the root and waiting
Rewriting the 40 service pages with an AI to refresh them
steps.feedback: Generative engines cite what answers the question, with information they can't find elsewhere. Without citable content, there's nothing to cite.

steps.prompt: The content is ready. How do you get the brand mentions that do the rest?
choices: Local press, trusted directories, customer reviews, even without a link
Posting comments on many forums, each with a link to the site
Paid links on foreign sites with high domain authority
Nothing: good content always ends up cited on its own
steps.feedback: An LLM associates a brand with a topic through the frequency and quality of mentions in its sources. Recognized directories and local press carry a lot of weight for a location-based query.

steps.prompt: How do you prove to the client that it works?
choices: Tracking the weekly citation rate on 30 questions asked to AIs
Counting the pages published since the start of the project
Tracking classic Google rankings on the client's keywords
A screenshot of ChatGPT citing the firm on a lucky day
steps.feedback: GEO is measured like SEO: a panel of queries, a frequency, a rate. Referral traffic from chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai in GA4 confirms it.

mkt-case-2:x:1.explain: Citable, original content → brand mentions → weekly measurement of citations.

mkt-case-2:x:2.title: The link building that went wrong
mkt-case-2:x:2.scenario: An e-commerce merchant bought 500 backlinks at €2 each on platforms. Six months later, Search Console shows thousands of links from Russian sites and empty directories, and organic traffic has been cut in half since the last anti-spam update.

steps.prompt: What do you do first?
choices: Audit the links to spot toxic domains and stop the purchases
Buy better-quality links to dilute the bad ones in the profile
Delete the site and start from scratch on a new domain
Wait for the next update: the traffic will come back by itself
steps.feedback: You stop the bleeding and qualify the problem before treating it. A new domain loses all the legitimate authority built up.

steps.prompt: What do you do with the toxic links?
choices: Request their removal if possible, then disavow the rest
Leave them in place: Google ignores them anyway
Redirect them to another page of the site to neutralize them
Buy other links to offset their negative effect
steps.feedback: Google says it ignores most spam links and reserves the disavow tool for sites that bought links at scale and risk a manual action: this is exactly that case. Removal first, disavow next.

steps.prompt: How do you rebuild a healthy link profile?
choices: Earned links: studies, tools, press relations, partnerships
A massive link exchange with friendly sites in the same niche
Blog comments with a link pointing to every product page
A network of satellite sites pointing to the store
steps.feedback: A quality link is one you would have gotten without SEO. Ten links from media and buying guides are worth more than a thousand directories, and they don't collapse at the next update.

mkt-case-2:x:2.explain: Audit and stop, removal then disavow, rebuild through earned links.

mkt-case-2:x:3.title: Internal linking on a large site
mkt-case-2:x:3.scenario: A media site with 12,000 articles: new articles take weeks to get indexed, and the in-depth articles (the "pillars") don't rank despite their quality. The menu has 8 links, and articles only link to each other at random.

steps.prompt: What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: No topical hierarchy and poor internal linking between articles
Too many articles: Google penalizes sites with over 10,000 pages
Titles that are too long and get cut off in the results
Articles that are too recent, which Google holds back for a year
steps.feedback: On a large site, internal linking is the number one lever: it guides crawling and distributes authority. A pillar with no inbound links is invisible.

steps.prompt: What structure should you put in place?
choices: Topic clusters: each pillar linked to its satellites, and back
Add every single article to the site's main navigation menu
A link to the homepage at the bottom of every article
Sitewide footer links to the 200 most-read articles
steps.feedback: The cluster concentrates links on the page that needs to rank and makes the topic readable for Google, and for the AIs that summarize a site.

steps.prompt: How do you speed up the indexing of new articles?
choices: Link them from the homepage and pillars, with an up-to-date sitemap
Submit them manually one by one every day in Search Console
Publish less so Google has time to read everything
Block old articles in robots.txt to free up crawl budget
steps.feedback: Google discovers through links: an article linked from the homepage is crawled in hours, an orphan article in weeks. The sitemap helps, links decide.

mkt-case-2:x:3.explain: Architecture diagnosis, topic clusters, links from strong pages.

mkt-case-2:x:4.prompt: A pillar page has been in position 3 for a year, with excellent content. The competitor in position 1 has weaker content. The most likely difference?
choices: Authority: more quality links and mentions
Text length: their page has 500 more words
Button colors that keep visitors on the page longer
The domain name, which contains the exact keyword
mkt-case-2:x:4.explain: With comparable content, authority decides. What's left is finding out where their links come from: that's the starting point of a link building strategy.

mkt-case-2:x:5.prompt: Your client wants to "be number one on ChatGPT". What do you tell them?
choices: That there is no rank: you aim to be cited often, and measure it
That they need to pay OpenAI to appear at the top of answers
That it's impossible, since AI answers are completely random
That adding an llms.txt file at the root of the site is enough
mkt-case-2:x:5.explain: GEO is about citation frequency, not rank. Setting the right indicator from the start avoids disappointment.

mkt-case-2:x:6.prompt: A text based on original data is more likely to be cited by an AI than a text that summarizes others.
choices: True
False
mkt-case-2:x:6.explain: Information gain: the model has no reason to cite a source that repeats what ten others already say.

mkt-case-3:x:1.title: ROAS in free fall
mkt-case-3:x:1.scenario: An online store spends €8,000 / month on Google Ads (Search + Shopping). ROAS has gone from 5 to 2.5 in three months. CPC has doubled on brand terms, and Performance Max absorbs 60% of the budget with "viewed" rather than clicked conversions.

steps.prompt: First check?
choices: Cannibalization between PMax and the brand campaigns
The budget, too low for PMax to exit the learning phase
The agency contract, to be changed before any analysis
Cutting all advertising while you figure it out
steps.feedback: PMax without exclusions takes brand queries, inflates CPC and takes credit for sales that would have come for free. Classic symptom.

steps.prompt: What do you put in place?
choices: Exclude the brand from PMax, isolate it and measure incrementality
Move the whole budget to PMax so the algorithm can optimize
Bid higher on brand terms to win back the top ad position
Remove the Shopping campaigns to concentrate the budget
steps.feedback: Separating brand and non-brand makes ROAS readable. An incrementality test tells you what advertising really brings beyond what would have come on its own.

steps.prompt: How do you then judge performance without being fooled by attribution?
choices: Track total revenue and marketing cost (MER), plus ROAS
Track the ROAS of PMax alone, since it is the biggest spender
Track impressions, which show your real visibility
Track the click-through rate of each ad, day after day
steps.feedback: A platform's ROAS grades itself by its own rules. The overall revenue / spend ratio doesn't lie.

mkt-case-3:x:1.explain: Brand / PMax cannibalization, separation and incrementality test, steering by MER.

mkt-case-3:x:2.title: The numbers don't add up
mkt-case-3:x:2.scenario: GA4 reports 320 purchases last month; the store actually took 410; Meta Ads claims 250 and Google Ads 190. Management asks "which one is right".

steps.prompt: Why does GA4 undercount?
choices: Cookie refusals and blockers: GA4 only sees part of the visits
GA4 is broken: you need to go back to Universal Analytics
The 90 extra purchases are fraudulent or test orders
The store is wrong: GA4 is the most reliable source
steps.feedback: The source of truth for sales is the back office. GA4 is a sample, useful for proportions, not for the total.

steps.prompt: And why do Meta + Google (440) exceed the real total (410)?
choices: Each platform claims the purchases it touched, even by a view
The platforms inflate their figures to sell more ads
A site bug sends each conversion to the pixel twice
Many customers end up buying the same product twice
steps.feedback: "Last click on MY platform" attribution + view-through conversions: adding up platforms always double-counts.

steps.prompt: What do you propose to management?
choices: Real sales as the reference, plus incrementality tests
Trust Meta, which reports the most conversions
Trust GA4, the most cautious and neutral of the tools
Add up Meta and Google Ads to get the real total
steps.feedback: You stop asking "who is right": you decide with real sales and experiments, and use the platforms to optimize within their own scope.

mkt-case-3:x:2.explain: GA4 samples, platforms double-count, the truth is in the till and in the tests.

mkt-case-3:x:3.title: An A/B test too good to be true
mkt-case-3:x:3.scenario: After 2 days and 600 visitors, variant B of the pricing page shows +38% conversion. The CEO wants to roll it out right away.

steps.prompt: Your opinion?
choices: Too early: 600 visitors and 2 days aren't enough
Roll it out right away: a +38% lift is a huge gap
Stop the test and keep version A, just to be safe
Add a variant C right away to speed things up
steps.feedback: A few conversions more or less make +38% on 600 visitors. You need the sample size calculated in advance and at least one full weekly cycle.

steps.prompt: How do you set the test duration?
choices: Calculate the sample size, then run until you reach it
Check every day and stop as soon as B pulls ahead
One week, always, whatever the traffic on the page
Until the CEO is convinced by the numbers
steps.feedback: Looking every day and stopping at the first "significant" result is the surest way to validate noise (peeking).

steps.prompt: The test concludes: B wins, p = 0.03. What is left to check?
choices: That the gain holds per segment, without hurting order value or churn
Nothing: p = 0.03, you can roll it out without further checks
That the CEO approves the variant before it goes live
That the product team also likes the design of B
steps.feedback: A variant can win on average and lose on mobile, or convert more customers who then cancel. You look one step further.

mkt-case-3:x:3.explain: Sample size before, no peeking during, segments and next metric after.

mkt-case-3:x:4.prompt: Your Meta campaign has a €12 CPA over the first 7 days, then €30 on the following days, with no changes. Most likely cause?
choices: Ad fatigue: the same creative, seen too often, wears out
Meta raised its prices for all advertisers that week
The product lost quality between the two periods
The Meta pixel stopped working on the site
mkt-case-3:x:4.explain: Frequency > 3-4 and falling CTR = fatigue. A broken pixel would make conversions vanish, not double the CPA. Remedies: new creatives, audience expansion, or a pause.

mkt-case-3:x:5.prompt: A client wants "a campaign that converts" with a €300 budget for a €2,000 product. What do you say?
choices: That €300 isn't enough: aim for a realistic lead goal
That it's doable on Search with the right keywords
That they need PMax, which optimizes on its own
That you can guarantee at least 5 sales this month
mkt-case-3:x:5.explain: A campaign needs enough conversions to learn: Google recommends at least a few dozen per month. With a €2,000 basket and €300, you measure leads, not sales.

mkt-case-3:x:6.prompt: If Google Ads shows 190 conversions and Meta 250, advertising generated 440 sales.
choices: True
False
mkt-case-3:x:6.explain: Each platform counts the conversions it touched, often view-through. The same sales end up in both columns.

mkt-case-1:x:6.title: The newsletter nobody opens
mkt-case-1:x:6.scenario: A weekly B2B newsletter: 12,000 subscribers, open rate down from 32% to 14% in a year, stable unsubscribe rate, no change in frequency.

steps.prompt: What do you check before touching the content?
choices: Deliverability and list quality (SPF, DKIM, inactive addresses)
The color and position of the newsletter's main button
The sending day, to be moved from Tuesday to Thursday
The length of the article titles in the newsletter
steps.feedback: A slow, steady decline with a stable unsubscribe rate points to an aging list and emails ending up in spam or in dead inboxes.

steps.prompt: The list contains 4,000 addresses with no opens in a year. What do you do?
choices: A re-engagement campaign, then remove those still inactive
Keep them all: one more send costs almost nothing
Email them twice as often to try to wake them up
Sell them to a partner to make the list pay off
steps.feedback: Mailbox providers judge reputation on engagement. Sending to dead addresses lowers deliverability for everyone.

steps.prompt: Once the list is clean, how do you bring the open rate back up?
choices: Test subject lines, segment by interest, keep a clear promise
Put "URGENT" in every subject line to create urgency
Switch to sending every day to stay top of mind
Add more images and GIFs to every newsletter
steps.feedback: Opens are earned over time: a recognized sender, a clear promise, content that delivers on it.

mkt-case-1:x:6.explain: Deliverability and list hygiene first, re-engagement, then subject lines and segmentation.

choices: Google
Apple

xAI
ia-9:x:3.explain: Gemini (Google DeepMind) was released in December 2023, replaced the Bard name in early 2024 and powers the AI Overviews in Google Search.

choices: Mistral AI
Hugging Face
Doctolib
Dassault
ia-9:x:4.explain: Mistral AI (Paris, 2023) releases open-weights models such as Mistral 7B or Mixtral. Hugging Face has French founders but was born in New York in 2016, and it is above all a model-hosting platform.

ia-9:x:5.prompt: What does "open-weights" mean for a model?
choices: Its weights can be downloaded and run locally
Its training code and training data are public
It is free to use via an API
It has no usage restrictions

ia-9:x:6.prompt: Llama is the family of open-weights models from…
choices: Meta
Amazon
Microsoft
IBM
ia-9:x:6.explain: Meta released Llama in 2023 and made open-weights models the core of its AI strategy.

choices: A database that finds the embeddings closest to a query
A classic SQL database with an index on every column
A giant spreadsheet where each row is a document
A JSON file listing the keywords of each text
ia-9:x:7.explain: Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector, etc.: they are used for RAG. Texts and the question are turned into vectors, the nearest neighbors are retrieved, and those passages are given to the model.

choices: A piece of text, often part of a word
Always a whole word, separated by spaces
A complete sentence, up to the full stop
Always a single character, letter or digit
ia-9:x:8.explain: In English, 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words. A model's context, price and speed are all counted in tokens.

ia-9:x:9.prompt: An LLM understands the world like a human and never gets facts wrong.
choices: True
False
ia-9:x:9.explain: An LLM predicts the next token. It can be extremely useful and completely convincing while being wrong: that is hallucination. Always check important facts.

ia-9:x:10.prompt: Put the main stages of building an LLM in order
steps: Collect and clean a very large text corpus
Pre-train the model to predict the next token (weeks of GPU time)
Refine it on examples of instructions and answers (fine-tuning)
Align it with human or AI feedback (RLHF / RLAIF)
Evaluate, red-team, then deploy behind an API
ia-9:x:10.explain: Data → pre-training → fine-tuning → alignment → evaluation and deployment. Pre-training costs the most; alignment is what makes the model usable.

ia-case-1:x:1.title: RAG or fine-tuning?
ia-case-1:x:1.scenario: Your company wants an assistant that answers customer questions based on 400 pages of documentation, updated every week.

steps.prompt: Which approach should you choose?
choices: RAG: fetch the relevant passages and give them to the model
Fine-tune a model on the 400 pages every week
Paste all 400 pages into the prompt of every question
Train an LLM from scratch on the documentation
steps.feedback: The documentation changes every week: RAG is updated by re-indexing, while fine-tuning would require retraining. And RAG lets you cite your sources.

steps.prompt: Some answers are made up. What should you do first?
choices: Require answers grounded in the passages, else "I don't know"
Raise the temperature to get more varied answers
Shrink each passage to a single sentence to keep it essential
Translate all the documentation into English before indexing it
steps.feedback: The system prompt frames the behavior: answer from the context only, cite, admit when there is no answer. Lowering the temperature also helps.

steps.prompt: How do you measure quality before going to production?
choices: A reference question set, scored automatically and by humans
Ask a colleague to try it out for five minutes or so
Track the number of tokens consumed per answer
Put it live and wait for customer complaints to come in
steps.feedback: An evaluation set (questions, expected answers, sources) lets you compare versions and catch regressions.

ia-case-1:x:1.explain: Changing content + need for sources = RAG. Then you frame the model and evaluate it against a reference set.

ia-case-1:x:2.title: Which model for which need?
ia-case-1:x:2.scenario: You need to automate three tasks: classify 50,000 incoming emails by category, write delicate replies to unhappy customers, and summarize 200 press articles every morning.

steps.prompt: To classify 50,000 emails into simple categories, you choose…
choices: A small, fast, cheap model, with few-shot prompting
The biggest model on the market, so no email is missed
A human team that reads and sorts every email by hand
A frontier model fine-tuned on all the emails
steps.feedback: Repetitive task, closed categories, huge volume: inference cost per call is what matters. A well-prompted small model gets the job done.

steps.prompt: For the delicate replies to unhappy customers…
choices: A frontier model, a strict system prompt and human review
The cheapest model, with the replies sent automatically
No AI at all: these messages are too sensitive to assist
